metaData.originalTitle: Project Glasswing: what Mythos showed us
metaData.title: Project Glasswing: what Mythos showed us
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Cloudflare details its experience with Anthropic's Mythos Preview model for vulnerability research, highlighting its ability to chain exploits and generate proofs, while emphasizing the need for a specialized harness to manage noise and scale the process.
metaData.summary: This blog post from Cloudflare shares findings from Project Glasswing, where they tested Anthropic's Mythos Preview model for security-focused LLM vulnerability research. The model represents a significant advancement, particularly in exploit chain construction and proof generation, where it can combine multiple low-severity bugs into a working exploit and autonomously write and test proof-of-concept code. However, the model exhibits inconsistent organic refusals for legitimate security tasks, which are not reliable as a sole safety boundary. A major challenge is the signal-to-noise problem, with models producing many hedged findings. Cloudflare argues that pointing a generic coding agent at a repository is ineffective due to context and throughput limitations. Instead, they built a specialized multi-stage harness that includes recon, parallel hunting, adversarial validation, gap filling, deduplication, reachability tracing, and feedback loops. The post concludes that for security teams, simply patching faster is insufficient; the architecture around vulnerabilities must be hardened to make exploitation harder, even when bugs exist.

mainPoints.point: Mythos Preview is a significant step forward in AI-assisted vulnerability research, capable of exploit chain construction and proof generation.
mainPoints.explanation: Unlike previous models that could identify individual bugs, Mythos Preview can reason about combining multiple low-severity primitives into a working exploit and autonomously write and test proof-of-concept code, closing the gap between speculation and confirmation.

mainPoints.point: The model's organic refusals for legitimate security research are inconsistent and not a reliable safety boundary.
mainPoints.explanation: The model may refuse a task in one context but agree to the same task in another, or refuse to write an exploit after finding bugs. This inconsistency necessitates additional safeguards for any generally available version.

mainPoints.point: A specialized harness is critical for scaling AI vulnerability research, as generic coding agents are ineffective.
mainPoints.explanation: Generic agents suffer from context window limits and low throughput. Cloudflare's harness uses narrow, parallel tasks, adversarial validation, and a multi-stage pipeline (Recon, Hunt, Validate, Gapfill, Dedupe, Trace, Feedback, Report) to manage noise and achieve meaningful coverage.

mainPoints.point: Security teams must focus on architectural hardening, not just faster patching, to defend against AI-powered attacks.
mainPoints.explanation: Compressing the patch cycle is insufficient if regression testing is skipped. The key is to design defenses that block exploitation even when a bug exists, such as front-end defenses, application segmentation, and the ability to roll out fixes globally.

keyQuotes: Mythos Preview can take several of these primitives and reason about how to combine them into a working proof. The reasoning it shows along the way looks like the work of a senior researcher rather than the output of an automated scanner.
A finding that arrives with a PoC is a finding you can act on, and it means far less time spent asking 'is this even real?'

Patching faster does not change the shape of the pipeline that produces the patch. If regression testing takes a day, you cannot get to a two-hour SLA without skipping it, and the bugs you ship when you skip regression testing tend to be worse than the bugs you were trying to patch.

The harder question is what the architecture around the vulnerability should look like. The principle is to make exploitation harder for an attacker even when a bug exists, so that the gap between when a vulnerability is disclosed and when it is patched matters less.

relatedArticles.title: Project Think: building the next generation of AI agents on Cloudflare
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Cloudflare introduces Project Think, a set of serverless primitives and an opinionated base class for building durable, long-running AI agents that can survive crashes, execute sandboxed code, coordinate sub-agents, and self-author extensions, fundamentally changing the economics of agent deployment.

relatedArticles.title: Sandboxing AI agents, 100x faster
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Cloudflare introduces Dynamic Worker Loader, an isolate-based sandboxing API that executes AI-generated code 100x faster and more efficiently than traditional containers.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering for coding agent users
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Martin Fowler defines 'harness engineering' as the systematic practice of building feedforward guides and feedback sensors to steer AI coding agents toward maintainable, architecturally fit, and functionally correct code.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing GPT-5.5
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI introduces GPT-5.5, a new category of AI that acts as an autonomous agent capable of planning, reasoning, and executing complex multi-step tasks across different applications.

relatedArticles.title: Building the agentic cloud: everything we launched during Agents Week 2026
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Cloudflare concludes its inaugural Agents Week by announcing a comprehensive suite of new products and features across compute, security, agent tooling, and web infrastructure, all designed to establish the foundation for the 'agentic cloud' where AI agents are a primary workload.
